---
title: "The Economist chart style guide: 2024 onward"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
## Fold each chunk's code behind a "Code" toggle; output stays visible.
local({
  source_hook <- knitr::knit_hooks$get("source")
  knitr::knit_hooks$set(source = function(x, options) {
    paste0("\n\n<details><summary>Code</summary>\n\n", source_hook(x, options), "\n\n</details>\n\n")
  })
})
```

```{css, echo = FALSE}
/* pkgdown gives every table Bootstrap's `table` class, whose cells are filled with --bs-table-bg (white); let the
   gt tables show their own background instead. */
table.gt_table { --bs-table-bg: transparent; }
```

*The Economist* redesigned its charts in March 2024, and has published no chart style guide since.
This article is a reverse-engineered replacement for *The Economist visual styleguide* (v1.2, 4 May 2017), which [another article](economist-2017-styleguide.html) reproduces.
It follows the sections of the 2017 guide and redraws its example charts in the new style.
It is not an official Economist specification.

The figures are *ggplot2* drawings made with `theme_economist_2024()`, `economist_2024_pal()` and the other 2024 tools in ggthemes.
The rules come from the public [Economist Design System](https://design-system.economist.com/) and [Marber color foundations](https://marber.economist.com/8e1dcf0b8/p/543b0f-colour/b/37fc5e), from a local corpus of post-redesign print charts and web graphics (cited by code, such as `20240406_BRC149`), and from recurring conventions in [Graphic Detail](https://www.economist.com/topics/graphic-detail) and the [weekly edition](https://www.economist.com/weeklyedition).

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
## The 2024 palettes, the theme at the guide's size and the drawing helpers, shared with the child documents.
source("economist-2024-guide.R")
```

## What changed in 2024

The redesign replaced the cool blue print ground and blue-first palettes with a warm gray print ground and red-first palettes.
Web charts remain white (see [A white ground with a short red tab](#a-white-ground-with-a-short-red-tab)).
The typeface changed too: ["Why has *The Economist* changed its typeface?"](https://www.economist.com/the-economist-explains/2024/02/07/why-has-the-economist-changed-its-typeface) (7 February 2024).

| Element | 2017 system | 2024 onward |
|---|---|---|
| Print ground | cool pale blue `#E7F0F5` | warm gray `#ECEBE0` |
| Web ground | white | white |
| First categorical color | blue | red |
| Supporting categories | blue, cyan, gold, teal | salmon, blue, light blue, dark gray, light gray |
| Text | black and blue-gray | near-black, with a gray source |
| Type | Econ Sans Condensed, 9.5pt headline | Economist Sans, a larger headline and subtitle |
| Top furniture | red tab; a full red rule on the web | a short red tab only |
| Panel headings | a short red marker | a short black rule |
| Number box | filled | outlined in black |
| Pie / doughnut | included | no longer used |

Print now also carries ribbons on lines, rank charts, highlighted scatters, forecast bands and dotted forecasts, log scales, a stacked area with a total line, lines with only event rules, ordered color ramps, and tables with boxed figures.

Unchanged: the right-hand value axis with labels above the gridlines, the black baseline with ticks below it, truncated years, unboxed panels, and a left-aligned headline over a subtitle giving measure and unit.

## Chart sizes

Print and web are separate compositions:

- **Print:** the whole graphic sits on warm gray `#ECEBE0`.
- **Web:** the whole graphic is white; it is built at three widths (700px, 550px and mobile), with labels and panels reflowing.
- **Alignment:** tab, headline, subtitle, plot and source share one left edge.

The figures keep the 2017 sizes (`economist_2017_size()`) and 7pt axis labels (`base_size = 7`); `theme_economist_2024()` sets every other size as a multiple of `base_size`.

## Typefaces

Standard charts use Economist Sans, which is not public: `economist_2017_font()` picks the closest installed substitute (Fira Sans Condensed, then Roboto Condensed, then `"sans"`).
Axis labels and source are light; pass a light family as `base_family` to match.

Footnotes are marked in the 2017 order.

```{r g24-footnote-symbols}
economist_2017_footnote(1:8)
```

```{r g24-footnote-figure, econ_size = "two_column", econ_height = 75}
## The label on the left over a rule, the eight symbols on the right, in the 2024 source gray.
g24_symbols <- data.frame(x = 0.36 + 0.08 * (0:7), number = 1:8, symbol = economist_2017_footnote(1:8))
g24_gray <- econ$print$source

g24_footnotes <- ggplot(g24_symbols, aes(x, 0)) +
  annotate("segment", x = 0, xend = 1, y = 1.15, yend = 1.15, colour = g24_gray, linewidth = 0.2) +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0.55, label = "Footnote symbols", hjust = 0, vjust = 1, fontface = "bold",
           colour = g24_gray, size = g24_pt(7.5)) +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0.05, label = "order of use", hjust = 0, vjust = 1, colour = g24_gray,
           size = g24_pt(7.5)) +
  geom_text(aes(label = number), size = g24_pt(7), hjust = 1, vjust = 0, nudge_y = 0.05, colour = g24_gray) +
  geom_text(aes(x = x + 0.006, label = symbol), size = g24_pt(14), hjust = 0, vjust = 0.5, nudge_y = -0.3) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-1, 1.8), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  g24_theme() +
  g24_no_axes()

g24_chart(g24_footnotes)
```

## Anatomy of a chart

A chart reads top to bottom:

1. a short red tab on the top edge, inset with the chart in print and flush left on the web;
2. a bold, sentence-case headline;
3. a subtitle giving geography, measure, unit and period, bold in print and medium on the web;
4. a key or panel heading, when needed;
5. the plot;
6. notes and source below the baseline.

The value axis sits on the right with labels just above the gridlines (`scale_y_continuous(position = "right")` with `guide_axis_economist_2017()`).
The baseline is black with ticks below it, the gridlines are pale, and there is no panel box.

```{r g24-anatomy-bare, econ_height = 165}
## Monthly yields, in years since the start: the 2017 guide's data.
tokyo_x <- c(1, seq(1.25, 13.5, by = 0.25), 13.7)
g24_bonds <- data.frame(
  year = rep(tokyo_x, 2),
  yield = c(
    4.7, 5.0, 5.2, 5.1, 5.6, 6.6, 6.7, 7.9, 6.8, 6.5, 6.7, 6.2, 5.7, 5.5, 5.4, 4.9, 4.6, 4.2, 4.5, 4.0,
    3.4, 3.9, 4.1, 4.5, 4.5, 3.9, 3.0, 3.0, 2.9, 3.2, 3.2, 2.9, 2.5, 2.5, 2.6, 2.1, 1.9, 1.8, 1.6, 1.1,
    1.5, 1.8, 1.6, 1.8, 1.8, 1.8, 1.7, 1.9, 1.6, 1.2, 1.2, 1.25,
    4.7, 5.2, 5.8, 5.9, 6.3, 6.2, 6.2, 5.8, 5.4, 5.0, 5.3, 4.7, 4.9, 5.2, 4.8, 4.0, 4.0, 3.8, 3.6, 4.3,
    4.2, 4.2, 4.6, 4.1, 4.2, 4.4, 4.1, 4.3, 4.4, 4.8, 5.1, 4.7, 4.6, 4.6, 5.0, 4.5, 4.0, 3.6, 4.0, 3.7,
    2.7, 2.8, 3.6, 3.4, 3.6, 3.7, 3.2, 2.6, 3.1, 3.4, 3.0, 2.3
  ),
  period = rep(c("January 1989 (Japan)", "January 1999 (US)"), each = length(tokyo_x))
)

g24_tokyo <- ggplot(g24_bonds, aes(year, yield, colour = period)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = g24_lw(1.5)) +
  g24_value_axis(limits = c(0, 8), breaks = seq(0, 8, 2), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(1, 13.7), breaks = 1:13, labels = ifelse(1:13 %in% c(1, 5, 10, 13), 1:13, ""), expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_colour_economist_2024("print") +
  labs(
    title = "Where Tokyo leads",
    subtitle = "Ten-year government-bond yields, %",
    x = "Years since start", y = NULL, colour = "Period beginning:"
  ) +
  g24_theme()

g24_tokyo
```

The theme sets the 2024 type and rules; three features are not theme elements:

* the **red tab** on the top edge;
* the **short black rule** over each panel heading;
* the **number box**, a square outlined in black at the top right.

`economist_2024_chart()` adds them to a finished plot and returns a grob.

```{r g24-anatomy-chart, econ_height = 165}
g24_chart(g24_tokyo + labs(caption = "Source: Thomson Reuters"))
```

## Source, footnote and number box

Put a note on its own line above the source, or ranged right on it.
A numbered box, a black-outlined square at the top right (filled in 2017), appears only in a numbered sequence.

```{r g24-anatomy-print, econ_height = 165}
fn <- economist_2017_footnote(1:2)

g24_chart(
  g24_tokyo +
    labs(
      subtitle = paste0("Ten-year government-bond yields", fn[1], ", %"),
      ## The commoner 2024 layout: the note on its own line above the source.
      caption = paste0(fn[1], "Annualised\nSource: Thomson Reuters")
    ),
  number = 1
)
```

Web charts have no red rule; the short tab is the only red furniture.

```{r g24-anatomy-web, econ_size = "two_column", econ_height = 190}
## Olympic medal sweeps; the 1996 games had none.
g24_sweeps <- data.frame(
  year = c(1948, 1952, 1956, 1960, 1964, 1968, 1972, 1976, 1980, 1984, 1988, 1992, 2000, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016),
  us = c(5, 6, 6, 4, 4, 6, 2, 4, 0, 1, 2, 1, 0, 2, 3, 0, 1),
  ussr = c(0, 4, 1, 4, 0, 0, 2, 3, 5, 0, 3, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0),
  eg = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 6, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0),
  other = c(2, 0, 3, 0, 0, 1, 4, 2, 0, 0, 3, 3, 2, 2, 4, 2, 0)
)
g24_sweeps <- data.frame(
  year = rep(g24_sweeps$year, 4),
  count = c(g24_sweeps$other, g24_sweeps$eg, g24_sweeps$ussr, g24_sweeps$us),
  country = factor(
    rep(c("Other", "East Germany", "Soviet Union", "United States"), each = nrow(g24_sweeps)),
    levels = c("United States", "Soviet Union", "East Germany", "Other")
  )
)

g24_anthem <- ggplot(g24_sweeps, aes(year, count, fill = country)) +
  geom_col(width = 2.7, position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +
  annotate("text", x = 1992, y = 1.55, label = "*", colour = "white", size = g24_text) +
  ## Red, salmon and blue for the three countries, light gray for "Other".
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "United States" = w24[["red"]], "Soviet Union" = w24[["salmon"]],
      "East Germany" = w24[["blue"]], "Other" = w24[["light gray"]]
    )
  ) +
  g24_value_axis(limits = c(0, 12), breaks = seq(0, 12, 2), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1948, 2016, 4), labels = economist_2017_year_format(), expand = c(0.01, 0)) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "National anthem monopolies", subtitle = "Number of “medal sweeps” by country",
    x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL,
    caption = "*Unified team of ex-Soviet republics\nSources: International Olympic Committee; Sports Reference; The Economist"
  ) +
  g24_theme("web")

g24_chart(g24_anthem, "web")
```

## Type scale and margins

`theme_economist_2024()` takes `base_size` as the axis-label size and sets the rest as multiples of it:

| Role | Treatment | Multiple of axis-label size | At `base_size = 7` | Theme element |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| Headline | bold, black | 20/15 = 1.33 | 9.3pt | `plot.title` |
| Subtitle | medium on the web, bold in print | 17/15 = 1.13 | 7.9pt | `plot.subtitle` |
| Panel heading | bold, under a short black rule | 1.13 | 7.9pt | `strip.text` |
| Axes, keys, annotation | light, black | 1 | 7pt | `axis.text`, `legend.text` |
| Source and notes | light, gray | 1 | 7pt | `plot.caption` |

- Axis labels are black, not gray, and the source is the same size.
- Print charts have a small outer inset; web charts none.
- Leave one line of clear space between subtitle or key and the marks.

### Leader block

Leader charts drop the tab and set the headline in red, as a single line naming the measure.

```{r g24-leader, econ_size = "leader"}
## Monthly, January 2011 to mid-2015.
g24_leader_data <- data.frame(
  year = c(2011.02, 2011 + (1:55) / 12),
  change = c(
    1.47, 1.56, 1.85, 2.19, 2.58, 2.69, 2.72, 2.81, 2.88, 2.84, 2.73, 2.61, 2.54, 2.54, 2.45, 2.19,
    1.85, 1.62, 1.52, 1.49, 1.63, 1.82, 1.82, 1.67, 1.59, 1.61, 1.52, 1.25, 1.22, 1.42, 1.57, 1.51,
    1.31, 1.12, 1.13, 1.3, 1.4, 1.25, 1.24, 1.51, 1.71, 1.73, 1.7, 1.64, 1.53, 1.45, 1.28, 0.98,
    0.51, 0.21, 0.27, 0.22, 0.2, 0.29, 0.32, 0.33
  )
)
g24_leader <- ggplot(g24_leader_data, aes(year, change)) +
  geom_line(colour = single24[["print"]], linewidth = g24_lw(1.2)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 2, colour = "black", linewidth = g24_lw(0.5)) +
  annotate("text", x = 2015.95, y = 2.08, label = "Fed target  2", hjust = 1, vjust = 0, size = g24_pt(6)) +
  g24_value_axis(limits = c(0, 3), breaks = c(0, 1, 3), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(2011, 2016), breaks = c(2011:2015, 2015.57), labels = c(economist_2017_year(2011:2015), ""),
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  labs(title = "US consumer prices,\n% increase on a year earlier", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  g24_theme(base_size = 6) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(colour = accent24[["print"]]))

g24_chart(g24_leader, tab = c(0, 0))
```

### Espresso lead image

```{r g24-espresso, econ_size = "espresso"}
g24_espresso_data <- data.frame(
  year = 2007:2015,
  change = c(4, 2, -5.7, 4.4, 6.8, 4.1, 2.9, 3, 0.9)
)
g24_espresso <- ggplot(g24_espresso_data, aes(year, change)) +
  geom_col(fill = single24[["print"]], width = 0.67) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "black", linewidth = g24_lw(0.5)) +
  g24_value_axis(limits = c(-8, 8), breaks = seq(-8, 8, 4), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2007:2015, labels = economist_2017_year_format()) +
  labs(
    title = "US retail sales",
    subtitle = "Excluding motor vehicles and parts,\n% change on a year earlier",
    x = NULL, y = NULL, caption = "Source: US Department of Commerce"
  ) +
  g24_theme(base_size = 6) +
  ## 120pt of chart, then 40pt blank, as in 2017.
  theme(plot.margin = margin(0, 6, 6 + 40, 6, "pt"))

g24_chart(g24_espresso)
```

### Panel chart

Panel headings are bold under a short black rule the length of the tab.

```{r g24-panel, econ_size = "two_column", econ_height = 195}
## The "Racy" chart: daily lines on the left, 12 points on the right.
panel_names <- c(
  "Donald Trump’s media dominance\nand polling surge",
  "Support for Trump v racial resentment\nand authoritarianism†,\nRepublican primary voters"
)
tv_mentions <- c(
  34, 29, 26, 35, 47, 56, 58, 55, 61, 64, 59, 55, 52, 52, 55, 58, 62, 61, 61, 58, 52, 50, 48, 53, 47, 41,
  41, 43, 42, 43, 47, 47, 48, 45, 35, 27, 27, 27, 27, 28, 37, 48, 50, 49, 57, 67, 63, 53, 55, 58, 56, 56,
  57, 57, 54, 54, 58, 57, 54, 45, 35, 35, 43, 48, 49, 53, 60, 64, 60, 60, 62, 69, 71, 69, 72, 70, 67, 69,
  71, 71, 71, 68, 70
)
polling <- c(
  3.8, 3.8, 4.1, 5.2, 6.2, 6.4, 9.3, 13, 16.7, 18.1, 19.3, 21.6, 23.6, 23.7, 22.5, 22.2, 22, 22.5, 24.4,
  26.5, 27.6, 28.8, 29.9, 30.4, 28, 24.8, 23.4, 23, 23.1, 23.4, 23.4, 24.8, 26.7, 27, 26.9, 25.7, 24.8,
  24.8, 24.5, 24.4, 26.1, 27.8, 28.6, 29.5, 29.8, 30.2, 31.6, 33.8, 34.5, 36, 35.5, 34.9, 34.6, 34.5,
  34.5, 34.7, 34.7, 35.7, 35.6, 34, 30.8, 29.3, 31.1, 33.6, 33.4, 33.9, 35.3, 36.2, 36.2, 34.1, 34.8,
  39.4, 42.9, 42.3, 41.4, 40.2, 39.3, 39.7, 40.4, 40.7, 42.2, 43.6, 45.3
)
days <- (6 * seq_along(tv_mentions) - 22) / 1.57
g24_panel_data <- rbind(
  data.frame(panel = panel_names[1], x = days, series = "TV mentions", value = tv_mentions),
  ## The polling average has its own 0-50 axis, so it is drawn at twice its value.
  data.frame(panel = panel_names[1], x = days, series = "Polling average", value = 2 * polling),
  data.frame(
    panel = panel_names[2], x = 1:12, series = "Authoritarianism",
    value = c(43.5, 42.9, 42.6, 43.5, 44.4, 45.3, 46.4, 47.7, 48.9, 49.9, 50.4, 50.6)
  ),
  data.frame(
    panel = panel_names[2], x = 1:12, series = "Racial resentment",
    value = c(2, 9.5, 17.3, 24.9, 31.4, 35.3, 39.1, 43, 46.5, 50, 53.5, 56)
  )
)
g24_panel_data$panel <- factor(g24_panel_data$panel, levels = panel_names)

## The two lines of each panel: red and blue, so that each colored axis reads apart from the other.
g24_first <- p24[["red"]]
g24_second <- p24[["blue"]]
g24_note <- econ$print$source
g24_panel_plot <- function(panel_pt) {
  up1 <- 100 / panel_pt # data units of the first panel per point
  up2 <- 60 / panel_pt
  txt <- function(data, size = g24_size) {
    geom_text(
      data = data, aes(.data$x, .data$y, label = .data$label, hjust = .data$hjust), colour = data$colour,
      size = g24_pt(size), inherit.aes = FALSE
    )
  }
  lab <- function(panel, x, y, label, hjust = 0.5, colour = "black") {
    data.frame(panel = factor(panel_names[panel], levels = panel_names), x = x, y = y, label = label,
               hjust = hjust, colour = colour)
  }
  axis_labels <- rbind(
    lab(1, -49.6, seq(0, 100, 20) + 4 * up1, seq(0, 100, 20), hjust = 0, colour = g24_second),
    lab(1, 342, seq(0, 100, 20) + 4 * up1, seq(0, 50, 10), hjust = 1, colour = g24_first),
    lab(2, 13.7, seq(0, 60, 20) + 4 * up2, seq(0, 60, 20), hjust = 1)
  )
  unit_labels <- rbind(
    lab(1, -49.6, 100 + 13 * up1, "TV mentions*, % of total", hjust = 0, colour = g24_second),
    lab(1, 342, 100 + 13 * up1, "Polling average, %", hjust = 1, colour = g24_first),
    lab(2, 13.7, 60 + 13 * up2, "Voter support, %", hjust = 1)
  )
  months <- lab(
    1, c(-4.4, 15.3, 46, 76.3, 105.5, 135.4, 165, 195, 226, 255.5, 285, 307.6), -9.5 * up1,
    c("J", "J", "A", "S", "O", "N", "D", "J", "F", "M", "A", "M")
  )
  years <- lab(1, c(86, 243), -19 * up1, c("2015", "2016"))
  direct_labels <- lab(2, c(1.2, 6.8), c(50, 32.5), c("Authoritarianism", "Racial resentment"), hjust = 0)
  scale_labels <- rbind(
    lab(2, 0.33, -9 * up2, "LOWEST", hjust = 0, colour = g24_note),
    lab(2, 12, -9 * up2, "HIGHEST", colour = g24_note)
  )
  scale_text <- lab(
    2, 7, c(-4.5, -13.5) * up2, c("Degree of authoritarianism", "Level of resentment"), colour = g24_note
  )
  scale_arrow <- data.frame(
    panel = factor(panel_names[2], levels = panel_names), x = 3.6, xend = 10.2, y = -9 * up2
  )
  ggplot(g24_panel_data, aes(.data$x, .data$value, colour = .data$series)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = g24_lw(1.2), show.legend = FALSE) +
    txt(axis_labels) +
    txt(unit_labels) +
    txt(months) +
    txt(years) +
    txt(direct_labels) +
    txt(scale_labels, 6.5) +
    txt(scale_text, 6.5) +
    geom_segment(
      data = scale_arrow, aes(x = .data$x, xend = .data$xend, y = .data$y, yend = .data$y), colour = g24_note,
      linewidth = 0.3, arrow = grid::arrow(ends = "both", length = unit(3, "pt"), type = "closed"),
      inherit.aes = FALSE
    ) +
    facet_wrap(~panel, nrow = 1, scales = "free") +
    coord_cartesian(clip = "off", expand = FALSE) +
    ## Set the panel ranges so the lettering outside the axes does not stretch them.
    scale_x_continuous(
      limits = function(limits) if (diff(limits) > 100) c(-49.6, 342) else c(0.326, 13.7), oob = scales::oob_keep,
      breaks = function(limits) {
        if (limits[2] > 100) c(-9, 0, 31, 62, 92, 123, 153, 184, 215, 244, 275, 305) else c(1, 12)
      },
      labels = function(breaks) rep("", length(breaks))
    ) +
    scale_y_continuous(
      limits = function(limits) if (max(limits) > 80) c(0, 100) else c(0, 60), oob = scales::oob_keep,
      position = "right",
      breaks = function(limits) seq(0, limits[2], 20)
    ) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(
      "TV mentions" = g24_second, "Polling average" = g24_first,
      "Authoritarianism" = g24_second, "Racial resentment" = g24_first
    )) +
    labs(title = "Racy", subtitle = "United States", x = " ", y = NULL) +
    g24_theme() +
    theme(
      axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.text.y.right = element_blank(),
      strip.text = element_text(margin = margin(3.5, 0, 18, 0))
    )
}

g24_chart(
  g24_panel_plot(60) +
    labs(caption = paste0(
      "*National news mentions of Trump compared with all Republican candidates\n",
      "†Poll Jul 30th-Aug 6th 2016\nSources: GDELT; RCP; YouGov"
    ))
)
```

Portrait panel charts stack the panels in one column.

```{r g24-panel-portrait, econ_height = 350}
g24_chart(
  g24_panel_plot(68) +
    facet_wrap(~panel, ncol = 1, scales = "free", axes = "all") +
    labs(caption = paste0(
      "*National news mentions of\nTrump compared with all\nRepublican candidates\n",
      "†Poll Jul 30th-Aug 6th 2016\nSources: GDELT;\nRCP; YouGov"
    ))
)
```

## Color

Color is semantic: red for focus, salmon for related or less emphatic categories, blue and light blue for the main contrast, grays for context.
Use only as many as needed; ordered categories take a ramp (see [Ordered categories](#ordered-categories)).

The palettes are provisional: the print set rests largely on one chart, and the ramps are reconstructions.

```{r g24-swatches, econ_size = "two_column", econ_height = 230}
## The palettes, grouped as the 2017 guide groups its swatches.
g24_swatch_rows <- list(
  list("PRINT", p24),
  list("WEB", w24),
  list("REDS", c(
    "print emphasis" = accent24[["print"]], "print single" = single24[["print"]],
    "web emphasis" = accent24[["web"]], "web single" = single24[["web"]]
  )),
  list("BACKGROUND", c(
    "print ground" = econ$print$bg$value[1], "print panel alt" = econ$print$bg$value[2],
    "web ground" = econ$web$bg$value[1]
  )),
  list("NEUTRAL", c(
    "print grid" = econ$print$grid, "print text" = econ$print$text, "print source" = econ$print$source,
    "web grid" = econ$web$grid, "web text" = econ$web$text, "web source" = econ$web$source
  ))
)
g24_swatch_data <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(g24_swatch_rows), function(r) {
  hex <- g24_swatch_rows[[r]][[2]]
  data.frame(group = g24_swatch_rows[[r]][[1]], row = r, col = seq_along(hex), name = toupper(names(hex)), hex = hex)
}))

ggplot(g24_swatch_data, aes(col, -row)) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = hex), width = 0.94, height = 0.42, colour = econ$web$grid, linewidth = 0.1) +
  geom_text(aes(y = -row + 0.36, label = name), size = g24_pt(4), vjust = 0) +
  geom_text(aes(y = -row - 0.32, label = hex), size = g24_pt(4), vjust = 1) +
  geom_text(
    data = unique(g24_swatch_data[c("group", "row")]), aes(x = -1.2, y = -row, label = group),
    size = g24_pt(6), fontface = "bold", hjust = 0, inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-1.2, 6.6), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(title = "Chart palette, print and web", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  g24_theme("web") +
  g24_no_axes()
```

### Qualitative palettes

The six-color order is **red, salmon, blue, light blue, dark gray, light gray**.
`economist_2024_pal(media)` returns it, and `scale_colour_economist_2024()` and `scale_fill_economist_2024()` use it.
The print colors are `r paste(unname(p24), collapse = ", ")`; the web colors are `r paste(unname(w24), collapse = ", ")`.

### Two reds: emphasis and single series

Two reds are used, rarely together:

- **emphasis red** (`#ED1C24` in print, `#E3120B` on the web): the first series of several, a highlighted bar, an interval, an annotation;
- **single-series red** (`#F04F38` in print, `#F6423C` on the web): a plain one-color chart.

`economist_2024_pal()` returns the single-series red when asked for one color; two or more start with the emphasis red.

### Evidence for separate web and print values

Print and web values are distinct in the exported assets, not only in the backgrounds: web graphics contain the six web values and none of the print ones, and the reverse (for example `20260829_FNC090`).
The two sets are not conversions of each other (see below).
The web set is secure; the print set is less so beyond red and salmon, and its blues vary from chart to chart.

### Print values are CMYK builds

The print colors are not the web colors converted for press: any common press profile (SWOP, FOGRA39, GRACoL and others) misses the print color by a median CIEDE2000 of 5.2 to 5.8, no closer than the web colors themselves, and warm web grays cannot become neutral print grays.
Each print color is instead a simple CMYK build rendered through U.S. Web Coated (SWOP) v2, the profile used for the classic charts since 2015.
The red is 0/100/100/0, the brand guide's print spec for Economist Red (screen value `#E3120B`), which SWOP renders as `#ED1C24`.
The single-series red and salmon are tints of the same build, and the grays are black ink alone.
The web colors were chosen in RGB, from design system tokens; the two sets share roles and order, not values.

```{r g24-print-cmyk, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(
  econ$print$palette[c("name", "cmyk", "hex", "observed", "delta_e", "confidence")],
  col.names = c("Color", "CMYK", "SWOP rendering", "Observed", "CIEDE2000", "Confidence"),
  align = "llllrl"
)
```

The specs are inferences: the simplest build that reproduces each observed color.
Blue is less certain, and no build reproduces the text color.
The table is `ggthemes_data$economist_2024$print$palette`; `data-raw/economist_2024_swop.R` reproduces it.

Only part of the palette is an exact token in the [Economist foundation palette](https://design-system.economist.com/foundations/colour/palettes):

| Role | Web chart value | Print chart value | Relation to foundation colors |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Red | `#E3120B` | `#ED1C24` | web is exactly Economist Red; print is its CMYK build |
| Salmon | `#FBA493` | `#F8AB90` | neither is an exact foundation token |
| Blue | `#3A4DAC` | `#28479D` | related to Chicago blue, but not an exact token |
| Light blue | `#7892C5` | `#659BD2` | related to Chicago blue, but not an exact token |
| Dark gray | `#6A6654` | `#636466` | the web gray is warm; the print gray is black ink alone |
| Light gray | `#BEBCAB` | `#C6C8CA` | the web gray is warm; the print gray is black ink alone |
| Ground | `#FFFFFF` | `#ECEBE0` | web is London 100; print is close to, but not, Los Angeles 90 `#EBE9E0` |

The web grays include exact London tokens (`#F2F2F2`, `#D9D9D9`, `#B3B3B3`, `#0D0D0D`); the blues are only related to Chicago blue.

### Party colors

Parties take the palette where they can:

- the left takes red and the right blue, so America's Republicans are red;
- second parties and earlier terms take the paler partner (salmon, light blue);
- unaffiliated members and "others" take the grays;
- third parties go off the palette: amber for the liberal center, orange for Britain's Liberal Democrats, green, cyan, and navy, dark red or dark green where a further party needs its own hue.

The values below are print values.

| Color | Value | Parties |
|---|---|---|
| Red | `#ED1C24` | Trump (second term), Canada's Liberals, the European Left, Basque Socialists, Britain's Labour (as a line among many) |
| Single-series red | `#F04F38` | France's New Popular Front; Labour |
| Salmon | `#F8AB90` | Trump (first term), Socialists & Democrats |
| Blue | `#28479D` | Biden, Canada's Conservatives, National Rally, Britain's Conservatives, Spain's People's Party |
| Light blue | `#659BD2` to `#8AAFDC` | Obama, Bloc Québécois, France's Republicans, European Conservatives & Reformists |
| Dark gray | `#636466` | Unaffiliated (European Parliament) |
| Light gray | `#C6C8CA` | Others |
| Amber | `#FCB316` | Ensemble, Renew Europe, New Democrats, SNP (`#F9BE2A`) |
| Orange | `#F57F20` | Liberal Democrats |
| Green | `#71BF45` | Greens, EH Bildu; Plaid Cymru in a paler `#99CF87` |
| Cyan | `#2FC0D3` | European People's Party, Reform UK |
| Navy | `#222B76` | Identity & Democracy |
| Dark red | `#B7131A` | People's Party of Canada |
| Dark green | `#0A5115` | Basque Nationalist Party (PNV) |

### Sequential and diverging red and gray

Red is for a measure carrying the editorial focus, gray for neutral ordered context; both ramps run from light (low) to dark (high).
Use the diverging ramp only when the center has meaning: zero, parity, a target or an average.

The ramps are reconstructions, not sampled house ramps.

```{r g24-gradients, econ_size = "two_column", econ_height = 150}
## One row per ramp, low to high, in each medium.
g24_ramps <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("print", "web"), function(media) {
  spec <- econ[[media]]
  rbind(
    data.frame(media = media, ramp = "Red", step = seq_len(nrow(spec$sequential_red)), hex = spec$sequential_red$value),
    data.frame(media = media, ramp = "Gray", step = seq_len(nrow(spec$sequential_gray)), hex = spec$sequential_gray$value),
    data.frame(media = media, ramp = "Red-gray", step = seq_len(nrow(spec$diverging)), hex = spec$diverging$value)
  )
}))
g24_ramps$row <- paste(g24_ramps$media, tolower(g24_ramps$ramp))
g24_ramps$row <- factor(g24_ramps$row, levels = rev(unique(g24_ramps$row)))

ggplot(g24_ramps, aes(step, row, fill = hex)) +
  geom_tile(width = 0.94, height = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = hex), size = g24_pt(3.6), colour = ifelse(g24_ramps$step > 3, "white", "black")) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0.01, 0)) +
  labs(title = "Sequential and diverging ramps", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  g24_theme("web") +
  g24_no_value_axis() +
  theme(axis.line = element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_text(hjust = 0))
```

`scale_fill_gradient_economist_2024("red")` and `"gray"` use the sequential ramps, and `scale_fill_gradient2_economist_2024()` the diverging one; `guide_colourbar_economist_2024()` draws their key as the published charts do.

### Ordered categories

Ordered categories take a ramp in the same order, with the focus in red at one end (`20240420_EPC345`), and are named beside their lines rather than keyed.

```{r g24-ordered-setup}
## Measured on `20240420_EPC345`, the print values: the red and salmon are the palette's; the deep salmon and the
## four warm grays are not (the lightest is not the palette's light gray `#C6C8CA`, which this chart keeps for its
## gridlines).
g24_ordered <- c(
  "Gen Z" = p24[["red"]], "Millennial" = "#E27A5E", "Gen X" = p24[["salmon"]], "Boomer" = "#C3C2B5",
  "Silent" = "#A4A495", "Greatest" = "#8A897D", "Lost" = "#64625D"
)
```


## Production recipe

```{r g24-production-recipe, eval = FALSE}
p <- ggplot(data, aes(date, value)) +
  geom_line(colour = economist_2024_pal("print")(1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(guide = guide_axis_economist_2017(), position = "right") +
  labs(
    title = "A short headline",
    subtitle = "Geography, measure, unit and period",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = "*Note, if any\nSource: Organisation or dataset"
  ) +
  theme_economist_2024(media = "print", base_family = "Economist Sans")

economist_2024_chart(p, "print")
```

Before export, check:

- Does the headline name what matters?
- Are geography, unit, period and denominator present?
- Is this the simplest chart type that answers the question?
- Does red identify the intended focus?
- Are series labelled directly where practical?
- Do bars start at zero?
- Are uncertainty, forecasts and omitted periods explicit?
- Do headline, plot and source share a left edge?
- Has web output been checked at 700px, 550px and the mobile width?

## Method and limitations

The corpus holds print PNGs from 2012--2026 and web graphics from 2024--2026.
Exact colors were counted from indexed PNG color tables; `ai2html` files supplied type families, weights, sizes and artboard widths.
The print sample is uneven and thin after April 2024, when print images leave the web archive and charts were collected one by one.
The web sample is larger.
It establishes the ground, qualitative order and recurring grammar, but not every rare layout.
The later examples (ribbons, rank charts, highlighted scatters, log scales, dotted forecasts, boxed tables) were found outside the main survey.
Where a 2017 chart type is absent from the corpus, its 2024 version applies the general rules.
